site.name: tinyactors
site.tagline: Like SQLite, but for actors: statecharts that run in your process.

audience.name: Agent-platform engineer
audience.description: A senior backend engineer building a multi-tenant backend for AI agents, chats or realtime sessions, in Node.js or Bun, evaluating a runtime for one long-lived stateful unit per session or tenant.
audience.knows: Actor systems and Cloudflare Durable Objects; Rivet; XState; containers and serverless limits. Little SCXML.
audience.want: Whether it runs inside the backend they already have
Memory per actor and how many fit in one process, with the benchmark behind the number
Hibernation and snapshots for idle sessions
A code example before any concept
audience.task: npm install and run the first chart
Compare it with Rivet and Durable Objects
audience.objection: Another runtime or platform to operate?
Is anyone running this in production?
Will an agent really write good charts?

audience.name: Workflow developer who tests
audience.description: A backend developer, often in Python, whose long-running business logic (retries, timeouts, payments, multi-day waits) is hard to test and has been hand-rolled as state machines or considered for Temporal.
audience.knows: Temporal or Celery and their replay or retry models; pytest; the pain of sleeping in tests and of flaky timing.
audience.want: A simulated clock that runs a week of timeouts in milliseconds
The whole flow written down as states and transitions
Effects as events their code performs, so tests need no mocks of the world
Commands that check, compare and run charts in CI, with no program to write
audience.task: Write one workflow as a chart
audience.objection: Does it need Docker or a cluster like Temporal?
What survives a crash of the process?
Will the simulated run match production?

audience.name: Tech lead who approves dependencies
audience.description: An architect or tech lead deciding whether the team may depend on tinyactors across services, clients and devices (Node.js, Python, the browser, C), and accountable when it fails.
audience.knows: Reasons like sqlite.org's "when to use" page: what it is for, what it is not for. Knows SQLite, embedded libraries, and the cost of a new server.
audience.want: An honest "use it when, do not use it when"
The failure semantics of one process: what is lost, what a snapshot or migration keeps
One chart running the same everywhere
The test suite that backs "passes all"
audience.task: Write the case for the team
audience.objection: One process is one point of failure.
What happens to state when the host dies?
Are we locked in to this runtime or its chart format?
